Fix the universal machine in the definition. Number its steps from one, and put \[r_c=
 \begin{cases}
  2^{-t},&\textstyle\mbox{if the machine first halts on }c\mbox{ at step }t,\\
  0,&\textstyle\mbox{if it never halts}.
 \end{cases}\] The real number \(r_c\) is uniformly computable. To approximate it with error at most \(2^{-N}\), simulate \(N\) steps. If halting occurs, return \(2^{-t}\); otherwise return zero. A later halting time produces an error at most \(2^{-(N+1)}\). This approximation procedure does not decide whether \(r_c\) is zero.

In the unit disk take the identity map, the fixed rational point \(p_c=(0,0)\), and the nonempty open rectangle \[U_c=(-r_c,1/4)\times(-1/4,1/4).\] Since \(0\leq r_c\leq1/2\), this rectangle lies in the disk. It has uniformly computable endpoints and is uniformly effectively open; its endpoint description can be approximated to every prescribed accuracy. Nevertheless, \[\{\operatorname{Id}^n(p_c):n>0\}\cap U_c\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r_c>0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T_U(c)\mbox{ halts}.\] The orbit does nothing. All undecidability is carried by a boundary-membership question for the target.
